summary.text: Legendre’s formula reduces the strengthened divisibility to, for every prime power \(t\), a floor inequality whose extra term records whether \(t\mid 30n-1\). Reducing \(n\) modulo \(t\) gives \(j=\lfloor30(n\bmod t)/t\rfloor<30\); in the divisibility case \(30(n\bmod t)=tj+1\) forces \(j\) to be odd and divisible by neither \(3\) nor \(5\), and a finite check of these residues supplies the extra unit, after which summing valuations and canceling the factorial denominator gives the result.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N_n=(30n)!\,n!,\qquad D_n=(15n)!(10n)!(6n)!,
\]
so that
\[
a(n)=\frac{N_n}{D_n}.
\]
We prove the stronger natural-number divisibility statement
\[
(30n-1)D_n\mid N_n                         \tag{1}
\]
for every \(n\ge 1\). This will both show that the factorial ratio is an integer and give the required extra factor \(30n-1\).

We begin with the floor inequality that drives the valuation argument.

### 1. A finite floor inequality

For every integer \(j\) with \(0\le j<30\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac j2\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac j3\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac j5\right\rfloor\le j.       \tag{2}
\]
Moreover, if \(j\) is odd and is divisible by neither \(3\) nor \(5\), then
\[
\left\lfloor\frac j2\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac j3\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac j5\right\rfloor+1\le j.     \tag{3}
\]

These statements involve only the thirty possible values of \(j\). For completeness, if
\[
g(j)=j-\left(\left\lfloor\frac j2\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac j3\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac j5\right\rfloor\right),
\]
then direct division gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
g(j)=1\quad&\text{for }j\in
\{1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,11,13,14,17,19,23,29\},\\
g(j)=0\quad&\text{for }j\in
\{0,6,10,12,15,16,18,20,21,22,24,25,26,27,28\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (2). The integers below \(30\) that are odd and divisible by neither \(3\) nor \(5\) are exactly
\[
1,7,11,13,17,19,23,29.
\]
They all occur in the first line, so their gap \(g(j)\) is \(1\), proving (3) (in fact with equality).

We now turn this finite assertion into an inequality valid for every modulus.

### 2. The inequality for an arbitrary modulus

Let \(t\ge 2\) and \(n\ge 1\). We claim that
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{15n}{t}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{10n}{t}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{6n}{t}\right\rfloor+
\mathbf 1_{\,t\mid 30n-1}
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{30n}{t}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac nt\right\rfloor,             \tag{4}
\]
where the indicator \(\mathbf 1_{\,t\mid 30n-1}\) is \(1\) when \(t\mid30n-1\) and is \(0\) otherwise.

Write the Euclidean division of \(n\) by \(t\) as
\[
n=tq+s,\qquad 0\le s<t.
\]
For each nonnegative integer \(c\), this gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{cn}{t}\right\rfloor
=cq+\left\lfloor\frac{cs}{t}\right\rfloor.      \tag{5}
\]
Set
\[
j=\left\lfloor\frac{30s}{t}\right\rfloor.
\]
Since \(0\le s<t\), we have \(0\le j<30\). Using the elementary nested-floor identity
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor x\rfloor}{d}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{x}{d}\right\rfloor
\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}),
\]
we obtain
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{15s}{t}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac j2\right\rfloor,
\quad
\left\lfloor\frac{10s}{t}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac j3\right\rfloor,
\quad
\left\lfloor\frac{6s}{t}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac j5\right\rfloor.             \tag{6}
\]
For example,
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{15s}{t}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{1}{2}\frac{30s}{t}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor30s/t\rfloor}{2}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac j2\right\rfloor,
\]
and the other two identities are analogous.

If \(t\nmid30n-1\), the indicator in (4) is zero. Equations (5) and (6) show that the two sides of (4), after cancelling their common contribution \(31q\), reduce to
\[
\left\lfloor\frac j2\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac j3\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac j5\right\rfloor\le j,
\]
which is (2).

It remains to handle the case \(t\mid30n-1\). Because \(t\ge2\), this divisibility is equivalent to
\[
30n\equiv1\pmod t.
\]
As \(n\equiv s\pmod t\), it follows that
\[
30s\equiv1\pmod t.
\]
By the definition of \(j=\lfloor30s/t\rfloor\), the latter congruence implies the exact equality
\[
30s=tj+1.                                         \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, the remainder of \(30s\) on division by \(t\) lies between \(0\) and \(t-1\), and here it is \(1\).

Equation (7) imposes three useful restrictions on \(j\). First, \(30s\) is even, so \(tj+1\) is even and hence \(tj\) is odd. Thus \(j\) is odd. Second, \(3\nmid j\): otherwise \(3\mid tj\), while also \(3\mid30s\), contradicting \(30s-tj=1\). The same argument with \(5\) shows that \(5\nmid j\). Therefore \(j\) satisfies the hypotheses of (3). Once again cancelling the common term \(31q\) using (5) and (6), inequality (4) becomes exactly
\[
\left\lfloor\frac j2\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac j3\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac j5\right\rfloor+1\le j,
\]
which follows from (3). This completes the proof of (4) in both cases.

### 3. Comparison of prime valuations

Fix a prime \(p\). For a positive integer \(m\), let \(v_p(m)\) denote the exponent of \(p\) in its prime factorization. Legendre's formula says that
\[
v_p(m!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor.    \tag{8}
\]
Only finitely many summands are nonzero.

We also use the elementary identity
\[
v_p(M)=\sum_{i\ge1}\mathbf 1_{\,p^i\mid M}                    \tag{9}
\]
for every positive integer \(M\). Indeed, if \(v_p(M)=e\), then precisely the powers \(p,p^2,\ldots,p^e\) divide \(M\), so the sum on the right consists of exactly \(e\) ones.

Apply (4) with \(t=p^i\) for each \(i\ge1\). Since \(p^i\ge2\), it gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{15n}{p^i}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{10n}{p^i}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{6n}{p^i}\right\rfloor+
\mathbf 1_{\,p^i\mid30n-1}
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{30n}{p^i}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac n{p^i}\right\rfloor.          \tag{10}
\]
Summing (10) over all \(i\ge1\), and using (8) and (9), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
&v_p((15n)!)+v_p((10n)!)+v_p((6n)!)+v_p(30n-1)\\
&\hspace{35mm}\le v_p((30n)!)+v_p(n!).
\end{aligned}
\]
By additivity of valuations on products, this is
\[
v_p\bigl((30n-1)(15n)!(10n)!(6n)!\bigr)
\le
v_p\bigl((30n)!n!\bigr).                         \tag{11}
\]
This holds for every prime \(p\). Both integers in (11) are positive when \(n\ge1\), and comparison of every prime exponent is equivalent to divisibility. Consequently,
\[
(30n-1)(15n)!(10n)!(6n)!\mid(30n)!n!,
\]
which is the promised stronger statement (1).

### 4. Extraction of the factorial ratio

For \(n\ge1\), (1) means that there is a nonnegative integer \(k\) such that
\[
(30n)!n!=(30n-1)(15n)!(10n)!(6n)!\,k.
\]
Since the factorial denominator is positive, exact division by it gives
\[
a(n)=\frac{(30n)!n!}{(15n)!(10n)!(6n)!}=(30n-1)k.
\]
Thus \(30n-1\mid a(n)\) in the natural numbers, and hence also in the integers.

Finally, consider \(n=0\). Every factorial appearing is \(0!=1\), so \(a(0)=1\), while
\[
30\cdot0-1=-1.
\]
Of course \(-1\mid1\). Therefore, for every integer \(n\ge0\),
\[
30n-1\mid a(n),
\]
as required.
